title: He sold 10% of Apple for $800. Was it a mistake?
summary: Ronald Wayne walked away from Apple after 12 days. Hindsight says disaster. What he knew at the time says something else.
body: In April 1976, Ronald Wayne co-founded Apple with Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. He held 10% of the new partnership, wrote its partnership agreement and drew the company's first logo.
Twelve days later, he gave up his stake for $800.

The internet calls it the worst decision in history. But look at what he knew at the time. Jobs had borrowed money to fill Apple's first big order, about $15,000. In a general partnership, each partner can be personally liable for the business's debts. Wayne was older than his partners and owned a house and a car. They had far less to lose. If Apple failed, creditors could come after what he owned.
Asked about it again in 2026, Wayne said he has no regrets.
lesson: A decision can be sensible and still turn out badly. Judge it by what was known at the time, not by how it ended.
check_title: Before any partnership, loan or guarantee, ask:
check: If this goes wrong, what can they take from me personally?

title: Do 70% of lottery winners really go broke?
summary: It's one of the most-shared money stats online. We looked for the study behind it and couldn't find one.
body: "Seventy percent of lottery winners go broke." You've probably heard it. We went looking for the study behind it, and couldn't find one.
The figure is usually credited to the US National Endowment for Financial Education (NEFE). In 2018, NEFE said the statistic is not backed by its research.

So what does research actually show? A study of almost 35,000 Florida lottery winners compared people who won $50,000 to $150,000 with people who won under $10,000. The bigger winners were less likely to file for bankruptcy right after winning, but about 50 percent more likely to file three to five years later. The money delayed bankruptcy. It didn't prevent it.
In Sweden, researchers following large lottery winners found they reported higher life satisfaction for more than a decade after winning.
lesson: Sudden money doesn't fix money habits. If a windfall lands on you, slow down before any big decision.

check: Who measured it?
Where's the original?

title: Is the 10,000-hour rule true?
summary: Practise 10,000 hours and you'll be world-class. The scientist behind the original study said that's not what he found.
body: A 2008 bestseller made it famous: practise for 10,000 hours and you'll be world-class at anything.

But in the original 1993 study by Anders Ericsson and colleagues, 10,000 hours was an average, for the best violinists by age 20. It wasn't a threshold, and plenty of them had practised less. Ericsson later wrote that the popular rule misread his work.

In 2014, a review of 88 studies found practice explained about 12% of the differences in performance overall, and under 1% in professions. Practice matters, but how you practise matters more than how long.
lesson: Hours aren't the point. Focused practice, with feedback, is.
check: Am I practising, or just repeating?
Who is giving me feedback?

It was popularised by a 2008 bestselling book, based on a 1993 study by Anders Ericsson and colleagues of violinists.
Is the 10,000-hour rule true?

Not as a rule. In the original study, 10,000 hours was an average for the best violinists by age 20, not a threshold. A 2014 review of 88 studies found practice explained about 12% of differences in performance overall, and under 1% in professions.
What kind of practice works best?
Researchers point to deliberate practice: focused effort on specific weaknesses, with feedback, rather than simply repeating what you already do.

title: He failed 5,127 times. Then the experts said no.
summary: James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes of a bagless vacuum. The big manufacturers still turned it down, and their reason is the real lesson.
body: James Dyson wanted a vacuum cleaner that didn't need a bag. For about five years he built prototype after prototype in a shed behind his house, going deep into debt. Prototype number 5,127 finally worked.
Then the big vacuum makers said no. They earned a fortune selling replacement bags, and a bagless machine would have cut into that.
So Dyson licensed his design in Japan, and the royalties kept him going. In 1993 he launched his own machine in the UK. Within about 18 months it was the country's best-selling vacuum cleaner.
lesson: When experts say no, ask what they lose if you're right.

check: Who is saying no?
What would it cost them if I'm right?

How did Dyson succeed after being rejected?

title: She bet $5,000 on pantyhose. And kept her day job.
summary: Sara Blakely started Spanx with $5,000 of savings, no investors and her fax-machine sales job intact. Testing before quitting was the bold move.
body: Sara Blakely spent seven years selling fax machines door to door for the office supply company Danka, and was promoted to national sales trainer at 25. It was a steady job with a steady salary, and she kept it longer than most people would guess.

The idea came from a small problem. She wanted to wear white trousers without visible lines, so she cut the feet off a pair of control-top pantyhose and wore them underneath. It worked better than anything she could buy, and she saw a product.

She put about $5,000 of her own savings into it. She never took an outside investor; in her words, she started it "with five grand from selling fax machines." And she did not quit. For about two years she kept her job at Danka and worked on Spanx at night, researching fabrics and patents.

She only resigned after Oprah Winfrey picked Spanx as one of her "Favorite Things" in November 2000, a moment that helped drive sales. By 2012 Forbes put her on its cover as the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world.

In 2021, the investment firm Blackstone bought a majority stake in Spanx at a valuation of $1.2 billion, and Blakely stayed on as executive chairwoman. The famous part of the story is the billion. The useful part is the two years in between, when she tested the idea while her salary kept coming in. Forbes now estimates her net worth at about $1.3 billion.
lesson: The bold move wasn't quitting. It was testing first.
check_title: Before you bet your salary on an idea, ask:
check: What's the smallest test I could run while I still have my job?
What result would tell me it's time to jump?

Did Sara Blakely quit her job to start Spanx?
Not at first. She kept her job at the office supply company Danka for about two years and built Spanx at night, resigning only after Oprah named Spanx a Favorite Thing in November 2000.
How much was Spanx worth?
In 2021 Blackstone bought a majority stake in Spanx at a $1.2 billion valuation. In 2012 Forbes called Blakely the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world.

title: They could've bought Netflix for $50 million. Saying no made sense.
seo_title: Netflix's $50 million offer to Blockbuster: why it said no
summary: In 2000 Netflix offered itself to Blockbuster for $50 million. With what Blockbuster knew then, passing looked sensible. Here's what changed.
body: In 2000, Netflix co-founders Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph went to Blockbuster's offices in Texas to meet its CEO, John Antioco. Their offer was simple: buy Netflix for $50 million. Randolph later wrote that when the number was named, Antioco was "struggling not to laugh." Former Netflix CFO Barry McCarthy said Blockbuster "laughed us out of their office."

It is easy to mock that answer now, but look at what each side knew at the time. Blockbuster had about 9,000 locations at its peak and revenue in the $5 billion range. Netflix mailed DVDs to a small base of customers and was deep in losses; Hastings said the company was on track to lose at least $50 million that year. The dot-com bubble popped soon after. Paying $50 million for a money-losing website did not look clever.

Blockbuster did not ignore the internet either. It launched Blockbuster Online in 2004, and its 2006 Total Access plan, which let customers return mailed discs in stores, grew fast. In one quarter of 2007 Netflix lost 55,000 subscribers. Randolph has spoken about "how close Blockbuster came to actually winning."

What decided the race was less one meeting than what came after: leadership changes, pricing choices and debt. Hastings said in 2009, "If it hadn't been for their debt, they could have killed us." Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010. By 2020 Netflix had more than 183 million subscribers, after more than $20 billion of revenue in 2019.
The lesson is not that Blockbuster was foolish. It is that a small, struggling idea can still be pointing somewhere big, and that size today is a poor guide to where something is heading.
lesson: Don't judge an idea by its size today. Judge where it's heading.
check_title: Before you dismiss a small idea, ask:
check: If this keeps growing for five years, what does it become?
What would I have to believe for this to be worth far more than it looks?
keywords: Netflix offered to sell to Blockbuster
faq: Did Blockbuster really have the chance to buy Netflix?
Yes. In 2000 Netflix's co-founders Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph offered to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco declined.
Why did Blockbuster say no to buying Netflix?

At the time Netflix was a small DVD-by-mail company expecting to lose at least $50 million that year, while Blockbuster had revenue of around $5 billion and thousands of stores, and the dot-com bubble was about to burst.
When did Blockbuster go bankrupt?
Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010. Netflix's Reed Hastings later said Blockbuster's debt was a key factor in the outcome.

title: This label said no to the Beatles. Then it learned.
seo_title: Why Decca rejected the Beatles in 1962, and what came next
summary: On 1 January 1962 Decca auditioned the Beatles and chose another band. A year later the same boss signed the Rolling Stones. Here's the story.
body: On Monday 1 January 1962, a young band from Liverpool arrived at Decca Studios in West Hampstead, London, for an audition. Starting at 11am and over roughly an hour, the Beatles recorded 15 songs under the supervision of Decca's A&R man Mike Smith. Their manager, Brian Epstein, hoped it would lead to a record deal.

It did not. Another group auditioned that same day: Brian Poole and the Tremeloes. Decca's head of A&R, Dick Rowe, and Mike Smith chose them, partly because they were based close to London. Rowe later explained, "We decided it was better to take the local group," because they could be worked with more easily.

The line everyone remembers comes from Epstein's 1964 autobiography, which quotes Rowe as saying, "Guitar groups are on their way out, Mr. Epstein." Rowe denied ever saying it. Either way, the Beatles kept going. Epstein had the Decca tapes copied, and they reached George Martin, head of A&R at Parlophone, part of EMI. Martin offered the band an audition at Abbey Road, and the band went on to sign with Parlophone.

Here is the part that is told less often. In May 1963, on a recommendation from George Harrison of the Beatles, Rowe went to see a new band at the Crawdaddy Club. Decca signed them within the week. They were the Rolling Stones.

So the label that passed on the Beatles did not repeat the mistake. A single miss, judged with what you knew at the time, is not the end of the story. Ignoring what it teaches you is what makes it expensive.
lesson: A miss only costs you twice if you ignore it.
check_title: After a decision goes wrong, ask:
check: What did I know at the time, and what would I look for differently next time?
Where is the next chance that looks like the one I missed?
keywords: guitar groups are on their way out
Brian Poole and the Tremeloes Decca
faq: Why did Decca reject the Beatles?
After the 1 January 1962 audition, Decca chose Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, who auditioned the same day, partly because they were based close to London and seen as easier to work with.
Who said "guitar groups are on their way out"?
Brian Epstein's 1964 autobiography attributes the line to Decca's head of A&R, Dick Rowe. Rowe denied ever saying it.
Did Decca sign the Rolling Stones?
Yes. In May 1963, on a recommendation from George Harrison, Dick Rowe saw the Rolling Stones and Decca signed them within the week.

title: He invented the digital camera. His company shelved it.
seo_title: Steve Sasson's 1975 digital camera: why Kodak held back
summary: In 1975 Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first digital camera. Kodak saw no market and kept it quiet. Here is what they knew at the time.
body: Steve Sasson joined Eastman Kodak in June 1973, fresh from a master's degree in electrical engineering at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. Working in Kodak's applied research laboratory, he built a camera around a new electronic image sensor, a CCD. By December 1975, at 24, he had a working camera that needed no film.

It was not pretty. The prototype was about the size of a toaster and weighed roughly 3.6 kilograms (about 8 pounds). Its Fairchild sensor captured a black-and-white image of just 100 by 100 pixels, or 0.01 megapixels. Taking the picture took 50 milliseconds, but recording it to a cassette tape took 23 seconds. To see the photo, you played the tape back on a television set.

Sasson demonstrated it to Kodak managers. He later described their reaction as "curiosity and skepticism", and said "they did not like the word 'digital'." He told the New York Times they were convinced that no one would ever want to look at their pictures on a television. Prints were cheap and familiar, and Kodak dominated the photo market through film. Sasson was not allowed to discuss the camera publicly or show it outside the company, though Kodak was granted a US patent for it in 1978.

Judged by what was known in 1975, the caution made sense: the camera was slow, heavy and needed a TV. But the technology kept improving. Kodak launched its own digital camera about 18 years later, by which time the shift was well under way. In 2012 Eastman Kodak filed for bankruptcy, and it emerged in 2013.
Sasson's work was eventually celebrated. He received the US National Medal of Technology and Innovation in 2009, and the IEEE commemorated his camera as a Milestone.
lesson: If a new idea threatens your best seller, someone else will build it. Better to learn from it early than to be surprised by it later.
check_title: Before you dismiss a clumsy new idea, ask:
check: Am I judging it by how good it is today, or by how fast it is improving?
Am I saying no because it is weak, or because it threatens something I already earn from?
keywords: why Kodak shelved the digital camera
faq: Who invented the first digital camera?
Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first self-contained portable digital camera in 1975, working in Kodak's applied research laboratory.
Why didn't Kodak sell the digital camera in 1975?
Executives didn't see a market: the prototype weighed about 8 pounds, took 23 seconds to save each photo and needed a TV to view it, and Kodak's business was built on film.
How many pixels did the first digital camera have?
It captured black-and-white images of 100 by 100 pixels, or 10,000 pixels (0.01 megapixels), recorded onto cassette tape.

title: His game flopped. Its chat tool sold for $27.7 billion.
seo_title: Slack's origin story: how a failed game became $27.7B
summary: Stewart Butterfield's online game Glitch shut down in 2012. The chat tool his team built to make it became Slack, sold to Salesforce for $27.7 billion.
body: In 2009 Stewart Butterfield, already known as a co-founder of Flickr, co-founded a company called Tiny Speck. Its first product was Glitch, a quirky online game with hand-drawn 2D worlds. Glitch launched on 27 September 2011.

The game struggled from the start. Within two months the team pulled it back to improve the gameplay, and in November 2012 Tiny Speck announced that Glitch would close. The game world shut down on 9 December 2012.

But while building Glitch, the team had made something for themselves: an internal chat tool to talk to each other. After the game closed, Butterfield turned that tool into the company's product. He announced Slack in August 2013 and it became publicly available in February 2014. The name stood for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge". The company raised $17 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, and in August 2014 renamed itself Slack Technologies.

Slack grew quickly: its revenue rose from $105.2 million in 2017 to $400.6 million in the fiscal year ending January 2019. It listed on the stock market in June 2019, and on 1 December 2020 Salesforce announced it would buy Slack for $27.7 billion. The deal closed on 21 July 2021.

It was not the first time this happened to Butterfield. In 2002 he co-founded Ludicorp to build an online game called Game Neverending. The game never launched, but tools built for it grew into Flickr, which went live in February 2004 and was bought by Yahoo in March 2005. Twice, the side tool turned out to be the real business.
lesson: The tool you built to solve your own problem might be worth more than the project it was built for. When a plan fails, look at what you made along the way.
check_title: Before you write off a project that didn't work, ask:
check: What did we build for ourselves that others might need too?
Am I attached to the original plan, or to solving a real problem?
keywords: how Slack started from a failed game
faq: How did Slack start?

Slack began as an internal chat tool that Stewart Butterfield's team at Tiny Speck built while making the online game Glitch. After Glitch closed in December 2012, they turned the tool into a product, released publicly in February 2014.
How much did Salesforce pay for Slack?
Salesforce announced on 1 December 2020 that it would buy Slack for $27.7 billion. The acquisition was completed on 21 July 2021.
Did Flickr also come from a game?
Yes. Flickr grew out of tools built for Game Neverending, an online game from Butterfield's company Ludicorp that never launched. Flickr went live in February 2004 and Yahoo bought it in March 2005.

title: He started over at 65. On $105 a month.
seo_title: Colonel Sanders started over at 65: the KFC story
summary: A new interstate emptied Harland Sanders's Kentucky cafe. At 65 he sold it at a loss, hit the road with his chicken recipe and built KFC.
body: Harland Sanders was born in 1890 in Henryville, Indiana. By the 1940s he was running the Sanders Cafe in Corbin, Kentucky, a roadside restaurant beside a busy highway that became known for his fried chicken. In 1935 Kentucky's governor had made him an honorary Kentucky colonel, the title he kept for the rest of his life.

In 1952 he licensed his chicken recipe to Pete Harman, who ran a restaurant in Salt Lake City. Harman became the first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchisee. But Sanders's own income still depended on the cafe in Corbin, and on the traffic that drove past it.

In 1956 a new stretch of Interstate 75 opened and bypassed the town. Customer numbers plummeted. At 65, Sanders was forced to sell the cafe, and the auction brought far less than it was worth. He was left with his savings and a Social Security check of $105 a month.

Instead of retiring, he went on the road with his recipe, visiting restaurants and selling them the right to serve his chicken. It worked: by 1964 Kentucky Fried Chicken had more than 600 franchised outlets in the United States and Canada.

That year, Sanders sold the company to a group of investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey for $2 million in cash, plus a salary to stay on as the brand's ambassador, a role he kept for life. By 1980 the chain's stores were reporting more than $2 billion in sales a year.
lesson: Losing the plan you built is not the same as losing what you are good at. Sanders's cafe was gone, but his recipe and his skill at selling it were not, and those turned out to be the real business.
check_title: If your current plan stopped working tomorrow, ask:
check: What am I great at that other people would pay for?
Who could I sell it to this month, not someday?
keywords: never too late to start a business
faq: How old was Colonel Sanders when he started KFC?

Sanders licensed his recipe to his first franchisee, Pete Harman, in 1952. He turned franchising into his full-time work after he was forced to sell his Corbin, Kentucky cafe at 65, when a new interstate bypassed it in 1956.
How much was Colonel Sanders's Social Security check?
After selling his cafe at a loss, Sanders lived on a Social Security check of $105 a month while he travelled to sell his recipe to restaurants.
How much did Colonel Sanders sell KFC for?
In 1964, with more than 600 outlets, Sanders sold Kentucky Fried Chicken to investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey for $2 million, plus a salary to stay on as its ambassador.

title: He quit Wall Street to sell books online. His boss had one line for him.
seo_title: Jeff Bezos quit Wall Street: the regret test behind Amazon
summary: In 1994 Jeff Bezos had a top job at a New York hedge fund. His boss called his idea better for someone without a great job. Here's how he decided.
body: In 1994 Jeff Bezos was a senior vice president at D. E. Shaw, a Wall Street hedge fund in New York. His job was to look for new business opportunities for the firm. That May, at 30, he came across a report that internet use was growing by 2,300% a year.

Bezos started thinking about what could be sold online. He settled on books: a printed catalogue listing millions of titles would be far too big to mail, but a website could hold them all, and book data was already well organised.

When he told his boss, David Shaw, the two went for a walk in Central Park. Shaw said it sounded like a good idea, but a better idea for someone who didn't already have a good job, and asked him to think hard before giving up a senior role. Bezos took time to decide.

The test he used later became known as his regret minimisation framework. He pictured himself at 80 and asked which choice he would regret. He decided he would not regret trying and failing, but he would definitely regret never trying. If it failed, he said, he would have been a happy software programmer somewhere.

Over the July 4 weekend in 1994, Bezos and his wife drove from Texas to Seattle while he wrote the business plan on a laptop. They rented a house in Bellevue and turned the garage into a workspace, with desks made from wooden doors. Amazon opened to the public on July 16, 1995, and in its first 30 days it sold books in all 50 US states and 45 other countries.
lesson: When a choice feels stuck between safe and bold, picture yourself at 80 and ask which one you would regret not having tried.
check: Is there something you keep putting off that 80-year-old you would wish you had tried?
What is the smallest version of it you could try this year without risking everything?
keywords: how amazon started in a garage
should I quit my job to start a business
faq: Why did Jeff Bezos quit his job at D. E. Shaw?

In 1994 he read that internet use was growing 2,300% a year and wanted to start an online bookstore. He decided using what he called a regret minimisation test: at 80, he would regret not trying more than trying and failing.
What did David Shaw tell Jeff Bezos about Amazon?
On a walk in Central Park, Shaw said it sounded like a good idea, but a better idea for someone who didn't already have a good job, and urged him to be sure before leaving.
Where did Amazon start?
In the garage of a rented house in Bellevue, near Seattle. Amazon opened to the public on July 16, 1995 and sold books in all 50 US states in its first 30 days.

title: Facebook rejected him in 2009. Then it paid up to $19 billion for his app.
seo_title: Brian Acton: rejected by Facebook, then WhatsApp's $19B sale
summary: In 2009 Twitter and Facebook both turned down engineer Brian Acton. He joined Jan Koum on WhatsApp, which Facebook bought in 2014 for up to $19 billion.
body: In 2009 Brian Acton was an experienced software engineer looking for his next job. He had spent years at Yahoo and was applying to the fast-growing internet companies of the time.

Twitter turned him down. Then, in August 2009, Facebook did too. Acton posted about it publicly on Twitter. Instead of complaining, he wrote that it had been a great opportunity to connect with some fantastic people and that he was looking forward to life's next adventure.

That next adventure was already close. His friend and former Yahoo colleague Jan Koum had started a small messaging app called WhatsApp earlier that year. Acton joined him and became a co-founder. The idea was simple: messages that worked reliably on any phone, so friends and families could stay in touch wherever they lived.

WhatsApp grew fast around the world. In February 2014 Facebook, the company that had turned Acton down five years earlier, agreed to buy WhatsApp for as much as $19 billion, the largest acquisition of a venture-backed company at the time, as reported by The Next Web and BGR.

Rejection stories are easy to tell backwards, as if the ending was obvious. It wasn't. In 2009 Acton had no idea the small app would grow into one of the most used messaging services in the world. What stands out is how he handled the no: he didn't take it as a verdict on his future, didn't burn bridges, and moved straight on to the next door. Five years later, the company that had said no was the one making the offer.
lesson: A rejection is about one company's door at one moment, not about your future. Treat it as information and move to the next door.
check: Which rejection are you still treating as a verdict on yourself?
What is the next door you could knock on this week?
faq: Did Facebook reject the WhatsApp co-founder?
Yes. Brian Acton posted in August 2009 that Facebook had turned him down for a job; Twitter had also rejected him that year.
How much did Facebook pay for WhatsApp?
In February 2014 Facebook agreed to buy WhatsApp for up to $19 billion in cash and stock.
Who founded WhatsApp?
Jan Koum started WhatsApp in 2009 and Brian Acton, his former Yahoo colleague, joined as co-founder later that year.

title: Seven women, ₹80 and one rooftop: the Lijjat Papad story
seo_title: Lijjat Papad story: seven women, ₹80 and a rooftop
summary: In 1959 seven women in Mumbai borrowed ₹80 to make papad on a terrace. Lijjat now has more than 40,000 members who own it together.
body: In 1959, in the south of Mumbai, seven women who lived as neighbours wanted a way to earn their own money. They were good cooks, and papad, the thin crisp wafer served with Indian meals, was something they already knew how to make well.

They had almost no money to start with. The group borrowed ₹80, less than one US dollar at the time, to buy the ingredients, and began rolling and drying papad on the terrace of their building. There were no investors and no factory, just a recipe, a rooftop and a commitment to keep quality the same every day.

The way they organised it mattered as much as the product. Lijjat, officially Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, grew as a cooperative: the women who join become members and own the organisation together, rather than working for an outside owner. Members make the papad, share in the earnings and help run it.

That model spread. According to WIPO, Lijjat grew to more than 40,000 members across 62 branches in 17 Indian states, and in 2013 its turnover was about ₹650 crore, roughly US$100 million. The brand name and consistent quality helped it become one of the best-known papad brands in India and to sell abroad as well.

The story is often told as a business case, but its core is simple. Seven people with a skill, a tiny loan and a rule they stuck to built something tens of thousands of women now share. The money at the start was the smallest part of it.
lesson: You don't need big money to start something. You need a skill, a small first step and people who keep showing up.
check: Who are the two or three people who would show up for your idea every day?
What is the ₹80 version of your idea: the smallest test you could run this month?

WIPO reports more than 40,000 members across 62 branches in 17 Indian states. The women members own the organisation together.

WIPO reported a turnover of about ₹650 crore, roughly US$100 million, in 2013.

title: He missed by 25 seconds. Two years later he ran a marathon under two hours.
seo_title: Eliud Kipchoge: from 2:00:25 to the first sub-2 marathon
summary: In 2017 Eliud Kipchoge missed a two-hour marathon by 25 seconds. On 12 October 2019 in Vienna he ran 1:59:40, the first human under two hours.
body: For as long as the marathon has existed, two hours looked like a wall. The distance is 42.195 kilometres, and running it in under two hours means holding a pace of under 2 minutes 51 seconds per kilometre the whole way.

Eliud Kipchoge, a Kenyan runner and Olympic champion, set out to break it. In May 2017 he ran a specially organised attempt on the Monza motor-racing circuit in Italy, with teams of pacemakers. He finished in 2:00:25. He had missed by just 25 seconds.
He did not treat it as a failure. He went back to training and racing, and two years later he lined up to try again, with a team of 41 pacesetters organised into nine groups.

On 12 October 2019, at the INEOS 1:59 Challenge in Vienna, Kipchoge ran 1:59:40, becoming the first human to cover the marathon distance in under two hours. The run started on the Reichsbrücke bridge over the Danube and finished in the Prater park. It was not ratified as an official world record because the event used rotating pacemakers and other aids not allowed in a standard race, but it showed the barrier could be broken.
The detail worth keeping is the 25 seconds. A near miss can feel worse than a clear failure. Kipchoge used it as a measurement: proof he was close, and a map of exactly how far he still had to go.
lesson: Missing by a little isn't failing. A near miss tells you how close you are and what to fix next.
check: What did you almost do that you could try again with one change?
How far away are you, really, from the goal you gave up on?
faq: Who was the first person to run a marathon under two hours?
Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna on 12 October 2019 at the INEOS 1:59 Challenge.
Is Kipchoge's 1:59:40 an official world record?
No. It was a specially organised event with rotating pacemakers, so it was not ratified as an official world record.
How close did Kipchoge get in 2017?
At the Breaking2 attempt in Monza, Italy, in May 2017, he ran 2:00:25, 25 seconds outside two hours.

title: He lost almost everything. A year later, he invented instant noodles.
seo_title: Momofuku Ando: from losing everything to instant noodles
summary: In 1957 Momofuku Ando lost nearly all his wealth. After a year of experiments in a tiny shed, he launched Chicken Ramen in 1958, the first instant noodles.
body: Momofuku Ando was a businessman in Osaka, Japan. In 1957 a credit union he headed collapsed, and he lost nearly everything he owned. According to Nippon.com, the only thing he kept was a rental property in Ikeda, Osaka.

He was in his mid-forties and had to start again. He had long been interested in food, and he set himself a goal: a noodle that people could make at home quickly, that tasted good, kept for a long time and was cheap.

He built a small workshop behind his house, about 10 square metres, and spent roughly a year experimenting there, reportedly without taking a single day off. Batch after batch failed before he found a way to season and dry noodles so they were ready in minutes with hot water.

In August 1958, when Ando was 48, Chicken Ramen went on sale: the world's first instant noodles. His company became Nissin Food Products. In 1971 he followed it with Cup Noodles, noodles in a cup that only needed boiling water, which went on to sell around the world.

Ando's story is often remembered for the product, but the starting point is what makes it useful. He did not begin from a position of strength. He began after losing almost everything, with a clear problem, a tiny workspace and a year of steady, focused work.
lesson: Losing everything can be a starting line, not a finish line, if you pick one clear problem and give it focused, daily work.
check: What one problem could you work on every day for a year?
What is your version of a 10-square-metre workshop: the small space or time you already have?
faq: Who invented instant noodles?
Momofuku Ando, founder of Nissin, launched Chicken Ramen, the first instant noodles, in August 1958.
How old was Momofuku Ando when he invented instant noodles?
He was 48 when Chicken Ramen went on sale in 1958, about a year after he lost nearly everything in 1957.
When were Cup Noodles invented?
Ando's company launched Cup Noodles in 1971.
sources: Nippon.com, Andō Momofuku: An Inventor Who Used His Noodle to Change Global Food Culture

title: Homemade detergent at ₹3 a kilo: how Nirma beat the big brands
seo_title: Karsanbhai Patel: how Nirma started at ₹3 a kilo
summary: In 1969 lab technician Karsanbhai Patel made detergent in his backyard and sold it door to door at ₹3 a kilo. Nirma became India's best-selling detergent.
body: In 1969, Karsanbhai Patel was a chemistry graduate working as a lab technician in Gujarat, first at a cotton mill in Ahmedabad and then in the state government's Geology and Mining Department. In his spare time he began making detergent powder in the backyard of his home near Ahmedabad.
At the time, the leading detergents in India cost around ₹13 a kilo, a price many households could not afford. Patel priced his powder at ₹3 a kilo, about a third of the big brands.

There was no distribution network and no advertising budget. After office hours, Patel cycled through neighbourhoods and sold the hand-packed packets door to door himself. It was a one-man, after-work business, and he kept his job for about three years before going full time.

The low price found a huge market that the big brands had left behind. Within about a decade Nirma had become the largest-selling detergent in India, ahead of established names, and the business grew into a major Indian group.

The lesson is less about detergent than about who you build for. Patel did not try to beat the big brands at their own game. He served the many buyers they had priced out, and that overlooked market turned out to be the biggest one.
It is also a reminder that you do not need to quit everything on day one. Patel tested his idea in his spare time, sold it with his own hands, and only went full time once people kept buying.
lesson: Build for the people the big players ignore. An overlooked market can be the biggest one.
check: Who is your idea really for, and who is everyone else ignoring?
What could you offer at a third of today's price if you started small?
faq: Who founded Nirma?
Karsanbhai Patel, a lab technician from Gujarat, started Nirma in 1969 by making detergent in his backyard.
How much did Nirma cost when it started?
About ₹3 a kilo, when leading detergents cost around ₹13 a kilo.
How did Karsanbhai Patel sell Nirma?
He cycled door to door after office hours, selling hand-packed packets himself.

title: LEGO almost went broke. Doing less saved it.
seo_title: LEGO's comeback: from near bankruptcy back to the brick
summary: In the early 2000s LEGO was near bankruptcy, with twice as many different pieces as before. Going back to the brick made it the world's top toymaker.
body: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, LEGO tried to grow by doing more of everything: theme parks, video games and sets far from its core brick. Some complex sets cost more in parts than they sold for. According to Britannica, the company lost more than $300 million in 2003, and it was on the brink of bankruptcy.

Part of the problem was hidden in the product line. The number of different pieces LEGO made had grown from about 6,000 to more than 12,000, which made every set more expensive to design, make and stock.

In 2004 Jørgen Vig Knudstorp became chief executive, the first person from outside the founding family to run the company. He cut costs, sold control of the LEGOLAND parks, dropped products that strayed from the core and took LEGO back to building and play, cutting the number of different pieces sharply.
The focus worked. In the first half of 2014, helped by the success of The LEGO Movie, LEGO passed Mattel to become the world's biggest toymaker by sales.
It is a useful test for any crowded to-do list. Ask which of your projects are the real brick and which are the extras, then give the brick your best time and energy.
The turnaround is a lesson in subtraction. When a business, or a person, is overwhelmed, the answer is often not to add more but to cut back to the thing that works and do it better.
lesson: When you're drowning, do less, better. Cut back to what works.
check: What's one thing you could stop doing this week?
What is your 'brick', the core thing that works best?
faq: Did LEGO almost go bankrupt?
Yes. In the early 2000s LEGO was close to bankruptcy; Britannica says it lost more than $300 million in 2003.
How did LEGO recover?
From 2004 CEO Jørgen Vig Knudstorp cut costs and products and took the company back to its core brick.
When did LEGO become the biggest toymaker?
In the first half of 2014 LEGO passed Mattel as the world's biggest toymaker by sales.
sources: Entrepreneur, How Lego Came Back From the Brink of Bankruptcy
The Marketing Society, How LEGO rebuilt its core brick by brick

title: At 49, she quit a top banking job and started Nykaa
seo_title: Falguni Nayar: quit banking at 49, built Nykaa
summary: Falguni Nayar left her job as MD of Kotak Mahindra Capital and started Nykaa in 2012, at 49. Its 2021 listing made her India's richest self-made woman.
body: Falguni Nayar had a long, successful career in finance. She rose to become managing director of Kotak Mahindra Capital, leading its institutional equities and investment banking work.

In 2012, at 49, she left that job to start something completely different: Nykaa, an online store for beauty and personal care products. It meant a new industry and a new career at an age when many people assume the big moves are behind them.

Nykaa grew into one of India's best-known beauty retailers. In November 2021 the company listed on the Indian stock market. Its IPO was oversubscribed many times over, and the shares opened well above the issue price.
With the listing, Nayar became India's wealthiest self-made woman, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In 2021 she was also named EY Entrepreneur of the Year in India.

The point is not the wealth. It is the timing. Nayar started at 49 with decades of experience in business, finance and people. For her, experience was not a reason to stay put; it was the advantage she brought to the new thing.

Her story also shows that a late start is still a start. The years before were not wasted; they were preparation. If you have an idea you keep putting off because you think the window has closed, her path suggests asking a different question: what do you know now that you did not know at 25?
lesson: 49 isn't late. It's experienced. What you already know can be your edge in something new.
check: What would you start if age didn't matter?
Which skills from your current work would give you a head start?
faq: How old was Falguni Nayar when she started Nykaa?
She was 49 when she founded Nykaa in 2012.
What did Falguni Nayar do before Nykaa?
She was managing director of Kotak Mahindra Capital.
When did Nykaa go public?
Nykaa listed on the Indian stock market in November 2021.

title: Stephen King threw Carrie in the trash. His wife pulled it out.
seo_title: Stephen King's Carrie: the novel he threw in the trash
summary: Stephen King threw the first pages of Carrie in the bin. His wife Tabitha pulled them out. The paperback rights later sold for $400,000.
body: Before he was one of the best-known authors in the world, Stephen King was a young high school English teacher. Money was tight, and he worked summers in a laundry to make ends meet.
He started writing a story about a teenage girl called Carrie. After a few pages he decided they were bad and threw them in the wastebasket.
His wife, Tabitha, found the pages and pulled them out. She read them and left him a note telling him to keep going, because it was good. King went back to the manuscript and finished it.

Doubleday accepted Carrie and paid a $2,500 advance. It was published in 1974. Then his agent sold the paperback rights to New American Library for $400,000, an enormous sum for a first novel. The paperback sold more than a million copies in its first year.

It is worth noticing how ordinary the turning point was. There was no big break or lucky meeting, just a few crumpled pages, one person who believed in them, and a writer who listened and kept going. Most finished work survives a moment like that.

The story is a reminder that the person closest to a piece of work is often its harshest judge. A second pair of eyes can see what you can't, and the draft you are about to throw away might be the one.
lesson: What you're about to throw away might be the one. Let someone else read it first.
check: What draft, idea or project is sitting in your bin right now?
Who could you show it to before you give up on it?
faq: Did Stephen King throw Carrie away?
Yes. He threw the first pages in the wastebasket; his wife Tabitha pulled them out and told him to keep going.
How much did Stephen King get for Carrie?
Doubleday paid a $2,500 advance, and the paperback rights later sold for $400,000.
When was Carrie published?
Carrie was published in hardcover in 1974.
sources: Monster Complex, Flashback: Carrie by Stephen King (1974)

title: No brewery would hire her. So she built Biocon.
seo_title: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw: from a ₹10,000 garage start to Biocon
summary: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw trained as a master brewer but couldn't get the job in India. In 1978 she started Biocon in a garage with ₹10,000.
body: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw studied malting and brewing at Ballarat College in Australia. She topped her class and earned a master brewer qualification in 1975.
Back in India she looked for work as a brewer in Bangalore and Delhi, but nobody would hire her as a master brewer.
Instead of waiting for someone to say yes, she started something of her own. In 1978 she set up Biocon in the garage of her rented home in Bengaluru, with seed capital of ₹10,000.

The company grew from that garage into one of India's best-known biotechnology businesses. When Biocon listed on the stock market in 2004, its market value at the close of the first day of trading was about $1.11 billion, and she has called the listing a eureka moment that showed her what she had built.

If you have been turned down for a role you are trained for, the skill has not disappeared. Ask who else needs it, what product or service it could become, and what the smallest version would cost to start. Her first step was a garage and ₹10,000, not a perfect plan.
Her path is a reminder that a closed door can point somewhere better. The job she was refused would have used her training; the company she built instead used all of it.
lesson: If no one gives you the job, build the company.
check: Who said no to you, and what could you build instead?
What skill do you have that you could use on your own terms?
faq: How did Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw start Biocon?
She set up Biocon in 1978 in the garage of her rented home in Bengaluru, with ₹10,000 in seed capital.
Was Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw a brewer?
Yes. She trained in malting and brewing in Australia and qualified as a master brewer in 1975, but couldn't get hired as one in India.
When did Biocon go public?
Biocon listed in 2004 and closed its first day of trading with a market value of about $1.11 billion.

title: $50 from his dad. Shoes in his trunk. It became Nike.
seo_title: Phil Knight's $50 start: shoes from a car trunk to Nike
summary: In 1962 Phil Knight borrowed $50 from his father and sold imported shoes from his car trunk, grossing $8,000 in year one. That company became Nike.
body: In 1962 Phil Knight was fresh out of business school, with an idea and very little money. He borrowed $50 from his father and set up a company with one simple mission: import high-quality, low-cost athletic shoes from Japan.
There was no store and no warehouse. Knight sold the shoes from the trunk of his lime green Plymouth Valiant, driving to customers himself. In his first year, he grossed $8,000.

That is a tiny number for what came next. Knight kept going, year after year, and the little import business he started with $50 grew into Nike, the company he later described in his memoir, Shoe Dog.

The story is often told as if Nike was destined to be big. It wasn't. It began with one person, one borrowed sum and whatever would fit in a car. The early years were small and slow, and the only real advantage was that he started and didn't stop.

Try it on your own idea. Ask what the smallest working version would be: one product, one customer, one weekend. Then ask what you could sell, test or learn with only the money and tools you already have. The answer is usually more than you think, and starting small also means mistakes stay small while you learn.
If you are waiting for the perfect amount of money, the perfect office or the perfect moment, Knight's start is a useful reminder. Most big things begin small enough to fit in a trunk.
lesson: Start with what fits in your car. A small start you keep going beats a big plan you never begin.
check: What could you start this week with almost nothing?
What are you waiting for that you don't actually need?
faq: How did Phil Knight start Nike?
In 1962 he borrowed $50 from his father and began importing athletic shoes from Japan, selling them from the trunk of his car.
How much did Phil Knight make in his first year?
He grossed $8,000 in his first year of selling shoes from his car.
What book tells the Nike origin story?
Phil Knight's memoir, Shoe Dog, tells how the company began and grew.
sources: OPB, Literary Arts Archive Project: Phil Knight
Simon & Schuster, Shoe Dog by Phil Knight

title: From talks to sell to Ford, to buying Jaguar from Ford
seo_title: Tata and Ford: from selling the car business to buying JLR
summary: In 1999 Tata held talks to sell its car business to Ford; the deal never happened. In 2008 Tata bought Jaguar Land Rover from Ford for $2.3 billion.
body: In 1998 Tata launched the Indica, its own passenger car. It was a bold move, but sales were slow at first.

Within about a year, in 1999, Tata held talks with Ford about selling its car business. Officials from Ford came to Bombay House, Tata's headquarters in Mumbai, to discuss it. The deal never happened.
So Tata kept the car business and kept building it. Nine years later the positions had changed. Ford, hit by the global downturn, was selling two of its British brands.

In 2008 Tata Motors bought Jaguar and Land Rover from Ford for $2.3 billion, paid in cash. The business it had once considered selling had grown into one strong enough to buy two of the world's best-known car brands.

It is worth asking the same question of your own work. Is the project you want to drop failing, or is it just early? Slow first-year numbers are normal for almost anything new. Before you sell, close or quit, compare where it is now with where it could be after a few more years of steady work.

The lesson is not about winning against anyone. It is about patience. Early results are not final results, and the project that looks weakest in its first year can turn into the base for something much bigger if you keep working on it.
lesson: The thing you nearly sold might be your future. Early results are not final results.
check: What are you about to give up on too early?
What would it take to give it one more year?
keywords: tata ford jaguar land rover story
faq: Did Tata try to sell its car business to Ford?
Yes. In 1999, after slow early sales of the Indica, Tata held talks with Ford about selling the car business, but no deal was made.
When did Tata buy Jaguar Land Rover?
Tata Motors bought Jaguar Land Rover from Ford in 2008.
How much did Tata pay for Jaguar Land Rover?
Tata paid $2.3 billion in cash for Jaguar and Land Rover.

title: Eighty years old, on top of Everest
seo_title: Yuichiro Miura: Everest summit at 80 after a broken pelvis
summary: Yuichiro Miura climbed Everest at 70 and 75, broke his pelvis skiing and had heart surgery, then reached the summit at 80 on 23 May 2013.
body: Yuichiro Miura of Japan first reached the top of Mount Everest at the age of 70. In 2008, at 75, he climbed it again.

Then came the setbacks. In 2009 a skiing accident broke his pelvis and his left thigh bone. He also had repeated heart problems: by January 2013 he had undergone four heart operations since 2007, the last one to treat an irregular heartbeat, only months before his next attempt.

On Thursday, 23 May 2013, at about 9 in the morning local time, Miura stood on the summit of Everest at 80 years old. That made him the oldest person to reach the top at the time. He called it the world's best feeling.
What makes the climb remarkable is not only the age. It is that he went back after injuries and surgery that would have given almost anyone a reason to stop.

You don't need a mountain to use the idea. Learning a language, starting a business, running a first race or going back to study all come with a voice that says it's too late. Miura's answer was to prepare, take the setbacks seriously and go anyway. Pick one thing you had written off and look at it again.
Most of us decide we are too old for something long before our body does. Miura's climb is a reminder to check whether a limit is real, or just a number we have accepted.
lesson: Your age is a number, not a limit.
check: What have you decided you're too old for?
What is one small step toward it you could take this month?
faq: Who climbed Everest at 80?
Yuichiro Miura of Japan reached the summit of Everest on 23 May 2013 at the age of 80.
Was Yuichiro Miura the oldest person to climb Everest?
Yes, at the time of his 2013 climb he became the oldest person to reach the summit.
How many times did Yuichiro Miura climb Everest?
Three times: at 70, at 75 and at 80.

title: She started her company at forty. And she almost didn't.
seo_title: Vera Wang started her company at 40: the late-starter story
summary: Vera Wang missed the Olympic team and the top job at Vogue. At 40 she feared it was too late, then opened her own bridal salon in 1990.
body: Vera Wang was born in New York in 1949 and started figure skating as a child. She competed at the 1968 U.S. Figure Skating Championships but did not qualify for the Olympic team, a result she has said left her devastated.
After graduating from Sarah Lawrence College she joined Vogue, where she became the magazine's youngest editor. She stayed for 17 years. When the editor-in-chief role opened, it went to someone else.

In 1987 she left Vogue for Ralph Lauren, where she worked as a design director for two years. Around 40, while planning her own wedding, she struggled to find a dress she liked. She later told CNBC that at the time she thought maybe it was just too late for her.
In 1990 she opened her first bridal salon in the Carlyle Hotel in New York. Her wedding dresses went on to become famous around the world, and the business grew far beyond bridal wear.

Starting at 40 also meant she did not start from zero. She knew fabric, fit and fashion from her years at Vogue and Ralph Lauren, and she knew exactly what she had been unable to find as a bride. That gap became her first product.

Her story is a reminder that missing one goal does not close every door. The skating, the years in fashion magazines and the time at Ralph Lauren all fed into the company she started at 40, so the detours turned out to be the training. If you are wondering whether it is too late, it helps to list what your earlier years have already taught you.
lesson: Your plan B can be the real plan.
check: What would you start if age didn't matter?
What have your past jobs taught you that you could build on?
faq: How old was Vera Wang when she started her company?
About 40. She opened her first bridal salon in New York's Carlyle Hotel in 1990.
Was Vera Wang an Olympic figure skater?
No. She competed at the 1968 U.S. Figure Skating Championships but did not qualify for the Olympic team.
How long did Vera Wang work at Vogue?
17 years. She became the magazine's youngest editor, and the editor-in-chief job later went to someone else.
sources: CNBC, Designer Vera Wang on starting her company at 40 (May 2021)

title: Two friends. One small flat. Selling books.
seo_title: Flipkart story: from a small flat to a $16 billion deal
summary: In October 2007 Sachin and Binny Bansal launched Flipkart as an online bookstore from a small Bengaluru flat. In 2018 Walmart paid $16 billion for 77%.
body: Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal, both IIT Delhi graduates who had worked at Amazon, launched Flipkart in October 2007 from a small flat in Koramangala, Bengaluru. There was no warehouse, no big office and no famous brand behind them.

Flipkart began as nothing more than an online bookstore. To find buyers, the founders stood outside a bookshop on Church Street and handed out Flipkart bookmarks to people walking out with new books. Their very first order was a single book, and it arrived a day late and not in perfect condition.

They kept going and kept fixing what went wrong. Once they had learned to sell and deliver books reliably, Flipkart moved into electronics, fashion, groceries and many other categories, and grew into one of India's biggest online stores. Each new category came after the last one worked, not all at once on day one.
In May 2018 Walmart announced it would buy a 77% stake in Flipkart for $16 billion, a deal that valued the company at close to $20 billion. It closed in August 2018.

The founders did not start with everything. They started with one category, learned how to do it well, and built from there. The bookmarks outside a bookshop are a reminder that the first customers often come from simple, hands-on effort rather than a big launch.
If you have an idea that feels too big, it can help to ask what the books version of it would be: the one product you could sell and deliver well this month.
lesson: Start with one thing you can do well.
check: What's the one thing you could start selling this week?
What is the smallest version of your idea you could launch?
faq: How did Flipkart start?
Sachin and Binny Bansal launched it in October 2007 in Bengaluru as an online bookstore, working from a small flat in Koramangala.
How much did Walmart pay for Flipkart?
Walmart paid $16 billion for a 77% stake in 2018, valuing Flipkart at close to $20 billion.
How did Flipkart find its first customers?
The founders handed out Flipkart bookmarks outside a Bengaluru bookshop to people leaving with new books.

title: Bankrupt. Then sold for four billion dollars.
seo_title: Marvel comeback: 1996 bankruptcy to Disney's $4 billion
summary: Marvel filed for bankruptcy in 1996 and sold film rights to its stars. It bet on the heroes it kept, made Iron Man, and Disney paid $4 billion in 2009.
body: In 1996 Marvel, the company behind some of the world's best-known comic-book heroes, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. It was deep in debt, and the comic business that had made it famous was struggling.

To survive, Marvel sold the film rights to many of its most popular characters to big studios. Spider-Man went to Sony, and other famous characters went to other studios. For a while it looked as if Marvel's future in film would belong to someone else.

Instead of giving up on movies, Marvel decided to make them itself with the heroes it still had. The first was Iron Man, released in May 2008. It grossed about $585 million worldwide and launched what became the Marvel Cinematic Universe. It was a bold step for a company that had so recently been through bankruptcy, and it became the start of what TheWrap calls Hollywood's biggest brand.

Success came fast. In 2009, only about a year after Iron Man, Disney bought Marvel for $4 billion. The company that once had to sell rights to survive had become one of the most valuable names in entertainment.

Marvel's turnaround did not come from getting back what it had lost. It came from taking the characters it still had seriously and building something new and well made around them, one film at a time.

The same idea works far outside Hollywood. After a setback it is tempting to focus on what is gone; the comeback usually starts with an honest list of what is still in your hands, and a decision to make the most of it. Ask what you can still build with it, starting this week.
lesson: Build with what you still have.
check: What do you still have that you're not using?
If you lost your biggest asset, what would you build with the rest?
keywords: marvel sold spider-man rights to sony
faq: When did Marvel go bankrupt?
Marvel filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 1996.
How much did Disney pay for Marvel?
Disney bought Marvel for $4 billion in 2009.
Why did Sony have the Spider-Man film rights?
Marvel sold Spider-Man's film rights to Sony while it was recovering from bankruptcy.

title: The first mile under four minutes. Run by a medical student.
seo_title: Roger Bannister: the first four-minute mile, 3:59.4 in 1954
summary: Roger Bannister finished fourth at the 1952 Olympics. Training about 30 minutes a day around medical school, he ran the first sub-four-minute mile in 1954.
body: Roger Bannister went to the 1952 Olympics in Helsinki as the favourite in the 1,500 metres. A change to the schedule added an extra round of heats, and he finished fourth, just outside the medals.

He was a medical student at Oxford, so his training had to fit around his studies. He kept it fairly light, about half an hour a day, and set his sights on a mark many thought was out of reach: a mile in under four minutes.

On 6 May 1954, at the Iffley Road track in Oxford, the day was cool, wet and windy. The wind dropped just before the start. With two friends pacing him, Bannister crossed the line in 3:59.4, the first mile ever run under four minutes.

What made the run possible was not a huge training load but a clear target. After the disappointment in Helsinki he could have stopped; instead he chose one specific goal, trained for it in the time he had, and used friends as pacemakers to share the effort on the day.
The record did not last long. Just 46 days later, John Landy ran 3:57.9. Bannister himself said he knew enough medicine and physiology to know the barrier was not a physical one.

Bannister went on to a long career in neurology and was knighted for his medical work. His run is still the classic example of a limit that only looked fixed until one person broke it. Once he showed it could be done, other runners stopped treating four minutes as a wall and started treating it as a target.
lesson: Limits break once someone goes first. Be the one.
check: What limit are you ready to break?
Which 'impossible' goal in your field has someone already broken?
faq: Who ran the first mile under four minutes?
Roger Bannister, on 6 May 1954 at Iffley Road in Oxford, in 3:59.4.
How long did Roger Bannister's mile record last?
46 days. John Landy ran 3:57.9 later that year.
How much did Roger Bannister train?
About 30 minutes a day, fitted around his medical studies.
